intents: keep a bad idea or habit going by passing it on to the next people
when parents repeat the same old stereotype and the kids grow up believing it too
make sure an unfair situation never ends, often without meaning to
keep a myth alive just by repeating it
ru_cue: не дать чему-то плохому закончиться, передавая его дальше

upgrades.plain: Laughing at those jokes only [keeps the stereotype alive].
upgrades.better: Laughing at those jokes only *perpetuates* the stereotype.

upgrades.plain: If nobody speaks up at the meeting, we'll just [keep the problem going].
upgrades.better: If nobody speaks up at the meeting, we'll just *perpetuate* the problem.

upgrades.plain: Every Christmas my uncle repeats the family myth that I failed my driving test five times, and Grandma [keeps it alive] by nodding along.
upgrades.better: Every Christmas my uncle repeats the family myth that I failed my driving test five times, and Grandma *perpetuates* it by nodding along.

collocations.chunk: only serves to perpetuate the cycle

ru_trap: Russian 'увековечить' sounds noble (a hero, a memory); *perpetuate* usually keeps something bad going, so to honour someone say 'keep their memory alive'.
nuance: Unlike *foster*, which helps something good grow, *perpetuate* keeps something (usually bad) going: myths, stereotypes, inequality.
personal: Which family myth do you think you still perpetuate without meaning to?
Which friend of yours perpetuates an old rumour every time your group meets?
hook: 'Пер-ПЕТЬ-ю-ate': a parrot that keeps singing (петь) the same old myth to every new generation.

intents: look at something very closely, hunting for any mistake or problem
when you go through a contract line by line before you sign, looking for a trap
examine every detail with a suspicious, critical eye
ru_cue: придирчиво изучать каждую деталь, выискивая ошибки

upgrades.plain: Before you sign, [look very carefully at] every page.
upgrades.better: Before you sign, *scrutinise* every page.

upgrades.plain: My mother-in-law [looked closely at] my cooking, just waiting for something to go wrong.
upgrades.better: My mother-in-law *scrutinised* my cooking, just waiting for something to go wrong.

upgrades.plain: The examiners will [check every figure in your report very carefully].
upgrades.better: The examiners will *scrutinise* every figure in your report.

nuance: Stronger and more critical than *examine*: you scrutinise something because you expect to find a fault.
personal: What is the last document you really had to scrutinise before signing?
Who in your family scrutinises your choices most closely?
gesture: Hold an imaginary magnifying glass up to your eye and lean in, frowning.
hook: 'Screw-tin-eyes': you screw up your eyes and stare at a tin until you find the tiny dent.

intents: completely rework a whole system instead of patching small bits of it
when the old booking system is so broken that fixing it piece by piece won't do
take something apart and rebuild it properly from top to bottom
ru_cue: полностью переделать систему сверху донизу

upgrades.plain: The school needs to [completely change] how it handles complaints.
upgrades.better: The school needs to *overhaul* how it handles complaints.

upgrades.plain: We spent the whole winter [taking apart and fixing] Dad's old car.
upgrades.better: We spent the whole winter *overhauling* Dad's old car.

upgrades.plain: After the third customer walked out in tears, the manager finally agreed to [totally rethink] the refund policy.
upgrades.better: After the third customer walked out in tears, the manager finally agreed to *overhaul* the refund policy.

nuance: Bigger than *streamline*: you overhaul when the whole thing needs rebuilding, not just simplifying.
personal: What part of your daily routine would you most like to overhaul?
Who do you know who completely overhauled their life after a big change?
hook: 'Over-HAUL': you haul the whole engine out over the side and rebuild every single part.

intents: make a process quicker and smoother by cutting out unnecessary steps
when signing up takes six forms and you squeeze it down to one
simplify the way something is done so it wastes less time
ru_cue: убрать лишние шаги, чтобы все шло быстрее

upgrades.plain: If we [cut some of the steps out of] the checkout, more people will buy.
upgrades.better: If we *streamline* the checkout, more people will buy.

upgrades.plain: She [simplified] her morning routine so she can sleep twenty minutes longer.
upgrades.better: She *streamlined* her morning routine so she can sleep twenty minutes longer.

upgrades.plain: I missed my flight because of the queue; they really need to [make the security checks quicker and simpler].
upgrades.better: I missed my flight because of the queue; they really need to *streamline* the security checks.

nuance: Unlike *overhaul*, *streamline* doesn't rebuild everything: it trims steps so the same thing runs faster.
personal: Which daily chore have you managed to streamline the most?
Who at your work or school could streamline how they do things?
hook: Picture water in a stream running in one straight line: no bends, no stops, just faster.

intents: something you've done so often that you no longer have to think about it
when you used to panic about changing gear and now your hands just do it
a skill so deep in your habits that it feels automatic
ru_cue: делать что-то так привычно, что даже не задумываешься

upgrades.plain: After a few months, typing without looking became [automatic] for me.
upgrades.better: After a few months, typing without looking became *second nature* to me.

upgrades.plain: For a nurse, washing your hands [is something you do without thinking].
upgrades.better: For a nurse, washing your hands is *second nature*.

upgrades.plain: I was so nervous at my first driving lesson, but now checking the mirrors [happens automatically].
upgrades.better: I was so nervous at my first driving lesson, but now checking the mirrors is *second nature*.

ru_trap: Russian 'вторая натура' carries over well; just say it's *second nature to me* (not 'for me'), with no article.
nuance: *Get the hang of* is the moment you start managing; *second nature* is much later, when you don't even notice you're doing it.
personal: What skill has become second nature to you that once felt impossible?
What is second nature to one of your parents that you still find hard?
hook: Picture a second you, born with the habit already built in, quietly doing the job while the first you daydreams.

intents: make someone decide not to do something because it looks risky, costly or unpleasant
when a barking dog in the garden makes burglars choose another house
put people off before they even try
ru_cue: сделать так, чтобы человеку расхотелось что-то делать

upgrades.plain: Cameras at the entrance [put off] most shoplifters.
upgrades.better: Cameras at the entrance *deter* most shoplifters.

upgrades.plain: The rain didn't [discourage] us from having the picnic.
upgrades.better: The rain didn't *deter* us from having the picnic.

upgrades.plain: Two rejections didn't [put her off]; she applied a third time and got the job.
upgrades.better: Two rejections didn't *deter* her; she applied a third time and got the job.

ru_trap: *Deter* takes 'from' + -ing (deter people from smoking), not 'to' or a plain infinitive as Russian 'отговорить делать' might suggest.
nuance: *Deter* works on a person's decision beforehand; *hinder* gets in the way once they've started.
personal: What once deterred you from trying something you later loved?
What would deter your best friend from moving abroad?
gesture: Hold your palm out flat towards someone, as if saying 'don't even think about it'.
hook: 'Deter' sounds like 'the terror': the terror of getting caught deters the thief.

intents: balance out a cost or loss with a gain of about the same size
when the train ticket costs more but you save all of it on parking, so it evens out
cancel out the bad side of something with a good side
ru_cue: уравновесить минус таким же плюсом

upgrades.plain: The higher rent is [balanced out] by not having to pay for travel.
upgrades.better: The higher rent is *offset* by not having to pay for travel.

upgrades.plain: I go running every morning to [make up for] all the cake I eat at work.
upgrades.better: I go running every morning to *offset* all the cake I eat at work.

upgrades.plain: Losing my bonus hurt, but it was more than [made up for] by the extra week of holiday.
upgrades.better: Losing my bonus hurt, but it was more than *offset* by the extra week of holiday.

ru_trap: Russian 'компенсировать' tempts 'compensate the cost'; English says *offset the cost* or 'compensate for the cost'.
nuance: *Mitigate* makes the harm smaller; *offset* leaves the harm but adds an equal gain on the other side of the scales.
personal: What do you do to offset a long week of sitting at a desk?
How does someone in your family offset a habit they feel guilty about?
gesture: Hold both hands out like scales; push one down, then the other, until they level.
hook: 'Off-set': one weight goes on, an equal weight is set on the other side, and the scales level off.

intents: jolt a group of people out of doing nothing and get them to act
when one shocking photo shakes the whole street out of doing nothing and sends everyone to clean the park
fire people up so strongly that they finally take action together
ru_cue: встряхнуть людей так, что они сразу берутся за дело

upgrades.plain: The news that the library might close [pushed] the whole town into action.
upgrades.better: The news that the library might close *galvanised* the whole town into action.

upgrades.plain: Losing 5-0 at home was what finally [got the team fired up].
upgrades.better: Losing 5-0 at home was what finally *galvanised* the team.

upgrades.plain: Her speech [stirred up] the volunteers, and fifty more signed up that night.
upgrades.better: Her speech *galvanised* the volunteers, and fifty more signed up that night.

ru_trap: Russian 'гальванизировать' is mostly technical or about reviving something dead; in everyday English you *galvanise people into action*.
nuance: A *catalyst* is the thing that starts a change; *galvanise* is the verb for shocking people into action, with a sense of sudden energy.
personal: What news has ever galvanised you into changing something straight away?
Who do you know who can galvanise a group just by speaking?
hook: 'Гальваника': a jolt of electric current runs through a sleepy crowd and everyone jumps up and gets moving.

intents: spread through every part of something, like a smell through a house
when damp soaks into the walls until the whole room smells of it
fill the whole of something so completely that it's in every corner
ru_cue: проникнуть во все уголки и пропитать целиком

upgrades.plain: The smell of burnt toast [spread through] the whole flat.
upgrades.better: The smell of burnt toast *permeated* the whole flat.

upgrades.plain: After the job cuts were announced, fear [filled every corner of] the office.
upgrades.better: After the job cuts were announced, fear *permeated* the office.

upgrades.plain: Water had [soaked right into] the old wooden floor.
upgrades.better: Water had *permeated* the old wooden floor.

ru_trap: Russian 'проникнуть в' tempts 'permeate into'; English usually takes a direct object: the smell permeated the house.
nuance: *Ubiquitous* says something is found everywhere; *permeate* is the spreading itself, seeping into every part of one thing.
personal: What smell permeated your childhood home?
Whose sense of humour permeates every family gathering you go to?
gesture: Start with your fingers bunched together, then slowly spread them outwards in every direction.
hook: 'Perm-eat': after one perm at the hairdresser's, the chemical smell permeates the whole salon for days.

intents: a lot of new things to pick up very quickly at the start
when you begin a new job and every single day there's a pile of new skills to master
that hard first stretch when you have to get up to speed fast
ru_cue: когда нужно очень быстро освоить много нового

upgrades.plain: My first month as a manager [meant picking up a huge amount very fast].
upgrades.better: My first month as a manager was *a steep learning curve*.

upgrades.plain: I nearly quit after my first week in the kitchen; [there was so much to pick up so quickly].
upgrades.better: I nearly quit after my first week in the kitchen; it was *a steep learning curve*.

upgrades.plain: This software [is hard to get used to at first], but it's worth it.
upgrades.better: This software has *a steep learning curve*, but it's worth it.

collocations.chunk: still on a steep learning curve
collocations.frame: I'm still on ___ with the new software

collocations.chunk: it was a steep learning curve

nuance: *Get the hang of* is reaching the point where you can do it; *a steep learning curve* is the hard, crowded stretch before that.
personal: When did you last face a steep learning curve?
Who do you know who handled a steep learning curve really well?
hook: Picture a ski slope so steep that you have to master turning before you reach the bottom.

intents: make two things that seem to clash fit together somehow
when your job and your family seem to pull against each other and you look for a way to make them fit together
make peace with someone after a long falling-out
make two sets of figures or two stories agree with each other
ru_cue: совместить то, что противоречит друг другу, или помириться

upgrades.plain: I can't [make his words fit with] his actions.
upgrades.better: I can't *reconcile* his words with his actions.

upgrades.plain: My dad and his brother finally [made up] after fifteen years of not speaking.
upgrades.better: My dad and his brother finally *reconciled* after fifteen years of not speaking.

upgrades.plain: How do you [balance] a full-time job with a newborn baby?
upgrades.better: How do you *reconcile* a full-time job with a newborn baby?

ru_trap: Russian 'примириться с' tempts 'reconcile with the loss'; English says *reconcile yourself to* it (or 'be reconciled to').
nuance: Unlike *see eye to eye* (simply agreeing), *reconcile* means bringing back together things or people that were in conflict.
personal: Which two goals of yours are hardest to reconcile?
Have two people you know ever reconciled after a long falling-out?
gesture: Bring two fists together and slowly lace your fingers.
hook: 'Reckon sail': 'I reckon we sail together,' says one old rival to the other, and they share one boat.

intents: a reward or benefit that makes people want to do something
when the company offers a bonus for finishing early, so suddenly everyone hurries
the carrot that gets people to act
ru_cue: выгода, ради которой человеку хочется что-то сделать

upgrades.plain: Free parking is a good [reason] to shop at the big supermarket.
upgrades.better: Free parking is a good *incentive* to shop at the big supermarket.

upgrades.plain: If nobody notices, I have no [motivation] to work harder.
upgrades.better: If nobody notices, I have no *incentive* to work harder.

upgrades.plain: My parents promised me a trip to Italy if I passed, which was a huge [push] to revise.
upgrades.better: My parents promised me a trip to Italy if I passed, which was a huge *incentive* to revise.

ru_trap: Russian 'стимул' tempts 'stimulus', but for a reason to act English says *incentive*: a tax incentive, not a 'tax stimulus'.
nuance: An *incentive* is offered on purpose to make people act; a *catalyst* is whatever happens to set a change off.
personal: What incentive would get you to wake up an hour earlier?
What incentive works best on a child you know?
hook: 'In-SENT-ive': the boss sent a bonus in the envelope, and suddenly everyone works faster.

intents: what everyone in a group finally agrees on
when ten friends argue for an hour about where to eat and at last all settle on one place
broad agreement across a whole group of people or experts
ru_cue: общее мнение, на котором сошлась вся группа

upgrades.plain: After a long debate, [the view everyone shared] was to cancel the trip.
upgrades.better: After a long debate, the *consensus* was to cancel the trip.

upgrades.plain: [Most doctors now agree] that sitting all day is bad for you.
upgrades.better: The *consensus* among doctors is that sitting all day is bad for you.

upgrades.plain: My family argued all through dinner, and the six of us never reached [an agreement we could all accept] on where Grandma should live.
upgrades.better: My family argued all through dinner, and the six of us never reached a *consensus* on where Grandma should live.

ru_trap: Russian 'достичь консенсуса' has no article; English needs one: *reach a consensus*.
nuance: A *consensus* is a whole group's agreement; *see eye to eye* is usually just two people agreeing.
personal: When did your family last fail to reach a consensus about something?
Who among your friends is best at building consensus in a group?
hook: Think 'common sense-us': it makes sense to all of us. Spell it con-SENS-us, not 'concensus'.

intents: a mismatch between two things that should be exactly the same, like two sets of figures
when the price on the shelf says one thing and the receipt says another
two stories of the same night that don't add up
ru_cue: несовпадение там, где цифры или факты должны сходиться

upgrades.plain: There's a [difference] between the price on the menu and the price on the bill.
upgrades.better: There's a *discrepancy* between the price on the menu and the price on the bill.

upgrades.plain: The police noticed a [mismatch] between his story and his sister's, and he went bright red.
upgrades.better: The police noticed a *discrepancy* between his story and his sister's, and he went bright red.

upgrades.plain: Could you explain [the gap in the figures] between the two reports? They're supposed to match.
upgrades.better: Could you explain the *discrepancy* between the two reports? They're supposed to match.

ru_trap: Russian 'расхождение в' and 'разница' push towards 'discrepancy of'; English says a discrepancy *between* two things or *in* the figures.
nuance: A *discrepancy* is a mismatch where things should agree (figures, accounts); a *disparity* is a big, often unfair gap between groups.
personal: Have you ever spotted a discrepancy on a bill or receipt?
Who do you know who would immediately notice a discrepancy in someone's story?
hook: 'Dis-crepe-ancy': two pancakes (crepes) on the plate should be identical, but one is twice the size, and you spot the mismatch.

intents: a situation where it's not clear whether something is allowed or not
when nobody can tell you if claiming your taxi home on expenses is OK or against the rules
something the rules don't clearly cover either way
ru_cue: ситуация, где непонятно, можно так или нельзя

upgrades.plain: Whether you can work from abroad on this contract is [somewhere between allowed and not allowed].
upgrades.better: Whether you can work from abroad on this contract is *a grey area*.

upgrades.plain: I wasn't sure if using my friend's discount code was cheating; it's [not exactly right, not exactly wrong], isn't it?
upgrades.better: I wasn't sure if using my friend's discount code was cheating; it's a bit of *a grey area*, isn't it?

upgrades.plain: Subletting your room for a few weeks [isn't clearly allowed or banned].
upgrades.better: Subletting your room for a few weeks is *a grey area*.

collocations.chunk: a bit of a grey area

ru_trap: Russian 'серая зона' tempts 'grey zone'; the usual English phrase is *a grey area*.
nuance: *Ambiguous* is about words or meaning; *a grey area* is about rules, or right and wrong, being unclear.
personal: What's a grey area at your work or school that people argue about?
Which friend of yours loves living in a grey area when it comes to rules?
hook: Picture a page half black, half white, and you're standing in the blurry grey strip in the middle where nobody can tell which side you're on.

intents: a big, unfair gap between two groups, like the rich and the poor
when men and women do the same job but one group gets paid far more
an unfair gap between groups of people, for example in pay, health or schooling
ru_cue: большой и несправедливый разрыв между группами

upgrades.plain: There's a huge [gap] in pay between the city and the countryside.
upgrades.better: There's a huge *disparity* in pay between the city and the countryside.

upgrades.plain: The [unfair gap] in exam results between rich and poor schools made the parents furious.
upgrades.better: The *disparity* in exam results between rich and poor schools made the parents furious.

upgrades.plain: It hurt to see the [gap] between how my parents treated my brother and how they treated me.
upgrades.better: It hurt to see the *disparity* between how my parents treated my brother and how they treated me.

collocations.chunk: a growing disparity between rich and poor
collocations.frame: a growing ___ between rich and poor

nuance: A *disparity* is an unfair gap between groups; a *discrepancy* is two things that should match but don't.
personal: What disparity between your town and the capital do you notice most?
Have you noticed any disparity in how your parents treated you and your siblings or cousins?
hook: 'Dis-PARITY': 'parity' means equal shares, like a fair 'пари' (bet), and 'dis-' breaks it: one side ends up far richer.

intents: what is likely to follow later as a result of a decision
when you hear 'we need to talk about your hours' and realise it really means you might lose your job
the meaning hidden behind words, suggested but not said out loud
ru_cue: то, к чему это приведет, или то, что подразумевается без слов

upgrades.plain: Have you thought about [what this will mean] for your pension?
upgrades.better: Have you thought about the *implications* for your pension?

upgrades.plain: I was hurt by the [hint] that I hadn't done my share of the cooking.
upgrades.better: I was hurt by the *implication* that I hadn't done my share of the cooking.

upgrades.plain: Nobody considered [what would happen] if the bridge closed.
upgrades.better: Nobody considered the *implications* of closing the bridge.

nuance: *Impact* is the effect itself; *implications* are what a decision may lead to, which you have to think through, or a meaning hinted but not said.
personal: What decision have you made without thinking through the implications?
Has someone you know ever said something with an implication that upset you?
hook: 'Im-PLY-cation': like layers of plywood, a second meaning is folded inside the words, waiting to be opened.

intents: a limit that stops you doing everything you'd like, such as time, money or space
a limit you have to work within, like a room only two metres wide when you wanted a big kitchen island
something that ties your hands and keeps your choices narrow
ru_cue: рамки, за которые нельзя выйти: время, деньги, место

upgrades.plain: Money is the main [limit] on where we can go on holiday.
upgrades.better: Money is the main *constraint* on where we can go on holiday.

upgrades.plain: We had to shoot the whole film in two days, so time was a real [issue].
upgrades.better: We had to shoot the whole film in two days, so time was a real *constraint*.

upgrades.plain: I'd love to help with the wedding, but with the new baby there are real [limits] on my time.
upgrades.better: I'd love to help with the wedding, but with the new baby there are real *constraints* on my time.

nuance: A *constraint* limits what you can do; a *drawback* is a disadvantage of something you already have.
personal: What's the biggest constraint on how you spend your free time?
What constraint does someone in your family work around every day?
hook: 'Con-STRAIN-t': in a straitjacket you strain and strain, but the straps won't let you move.

intents: the one downside of something that is otherwise good
when you love the new flat but there's no lift and you live on the fifth floor
the catch that spoils a great option a little
ru_cue: минус у вещи, которая в остальном хороша

upgrades.plain: The main [downside] of living in the centre is the noise.
upgrades.better: The main *drawback* of living in the centre is the noise.

upgrades.plain: I loved the dress, but the [catch] was that it cost half my rent.
upgrades.better: I loved the dress, but the *drawback* was that it cost half my rent.

upgrades.plain: Working from home is great; the one [disadvantage] is that I talk to nobody all day.
upgrades.better: Working from home is great; the one *drawback* is that I talk to nobody all day.

ru_trap: Russian 'минус' tempts 'the minus of it'; English says *the drawback* (or 'downside') of it.
nuance: A *drawback* is one weak point of something good; *a double-edged sword* has a good and a bad side so tangled you can't separate them.
personal: What's the biggest drawback of where you live now?
What drawback does a friend of yours always mention about their job?
hook: 'Draw back': the one thing that makes you draw your hand back at the last second before buying.

intents: a shock that makes you realise you must change something
when your doctor says your blood pressure is far too high and you finally start exercising
a nasty surprise that warns you things can't go on like this
ru_cue: тревожный сигнал, после которого понимаешь: пора меняться

upgrades.plain: Failing my mock exam was [a real shock]; I started revising every night.
upgrades.better: Failing my mock exam was *a wake-up call*; I started revising every night.

upgrades.plain: That huge phone bill was [a warning sign] about our spending.
upgrades.better: That huge phone bill was *a wake-up call* about our spending.

upgrades.plain: The flood should be [a warning] for the whole town.
upgrades.better: The flood should be *a wake-up call* for the whole town.

collocations.chunk: it was a wake-up call for
collocations.frame: it was ___ for all of us

ru_trap: Russian 'тревожный звонок' tempts 'an alarming call'; English says *a wake-up call* (or 'it set alarm bells ringing').
nuance: An *epiphany* is a sudden insight; *a wake-up call* is an unpleasant shock or warning that pushes you to change.
personal: What was a wake-up call that changed one of your habits?
Who do you know who needs a wake-up call about their health?
hook: Picture a hotel phone ringing at six in the morning: 'This is your wake-up call', and you leap out of bed to change your life.

intents: the event that sets off a big change
the single thing that triggers a much bigger change, like one online video that leads to new rules
the spark that finally gets a long-overdue change moving
ru_cue: то, с чего начинаются большие перемены

upgrades.plain: Losing her job was the [trigger] for starting her own business.
upgrades.better: Losing her job was the *catalyst* for starting her own business.

upgrades.plain: The fire was the [spark] for new safety rules across the city.
upgrades.better: The fire was the *catalyst* for new safety rules across the city.

upgrades.plain: My grandad's heart attack was [what started] a huge change in how our whole family eats.
upgrades.better: My grandad's heart attack was the *catalyst* for a huge change in how our whole family eats.

ru_trap: Russian 'катализатор чего-то' tempts 'catalyst of'; English usually says *a catalyst for* something.
nuance: A *catalyst* is whatever sets a change off; *galvanise* is the verb for jolting people into action; an *incentive* is a reward offered on purpose.
personal: What was the catalyst for the biggest change in your life so far?
What was the catalyst for a friend of yours changing career or city?
hook: 'Cat-a-list': the cat knocks your to-do list off the table, and that's what finally gets everything moving.

intents: the level you have to reach before something starts to happen
when you need to spend thirty pounds before delivery becomes free
the point beyond which a tax, a rule or pain begins to kick in
ru_cue: уровень, начиная с которого что-то начинает действовать

upgrades.plain: You only pay tax once you earn over a certain [amount].
upgrades.better: You only pay tax once you earn over a certain *threshold*.

upgrades.plain: My [ability to put up with] pain is embarrassingly low; I cry at injections.
upgrades.better: My pain *threshold* is embarrassingly low; I cry at injections.

upgrades.plain: Orders above the [minimum] of fifty pounds get free delivery.
upgrades.better: Orders above the *threshold* of fifty pounds get free delivery.

nuance: A *constraint* limits what you can do; a *threshold* is the point at which something starts: tax, pain, free delivery.
personal: What is your threshold for noise before you complain to a neighbour?
Who do you know with an amazingly high pain threshold?
gesture: Lift your foot and step deliberately over an imaginary line on the floor.
hook: Picture an old man threshing wheat on your doorstep: you have to step right over him before anything can begin.
